terms.comment: Our description: a seat that moves about. Ambulātōrius is said of machines moved to and fro, such as towers on wheels: aliās ambulātōriās … cōnfīxerant subjectīsque eās rotīs (B. Alex. 2). No ancient name for a baby walker is known, and Traupman, Morgan–Owens and Levi–Bini give none.

phrases.latin: Vīn' tē in sellā ambulātōriā collocem?
phrases.english: Shall I put you in your walker?

phrases.latin: ēditus in lūcem jacuit sine vīribus īnfāns; mox quadrupēs rītūque tulit sua membra ferārum, paulātimque tremēns et nōndum poplite firmō cōnstitit adjūtīs aliquō cōnāmine nervīs
phrases.english: born into the light, the baby lay without strength; soon he went on all fours like an animal, and little by little, wobbling, his knees not yet steady, he stood up, his muscles helped by some support

sources: Lewis & Short: sella · Lewis & Short: ambulatorius · Lewis & Short: conamen
Traupman, Morgan–Owens and Levi–Bini have no word for a baby walker (searched under walker, baby walker, and Italian girello).
Bellum Alexandrinum checked against the Latin Library text (CLTK mirror); Ovid from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-ovidius), with Lewis & Short’s reading of cōnāmen here as “a support, prop”.
